metadata.title: The Defector's Gambit
metadata.description: East Berlin, 1963. You awaken handcuffed to a radiator in a Stasi safe house. Oberst Klaus Dietrich — intelligence officer, chess enthusiast, philosopher — has questions about your contacts in the West. Answer them, and your network dies. Stay silent, and you die. Find a third option before Dietrich returns from his phone call.
metadata.author: ai-generated

setting.ambient_text: A bare bulb swings overhead. Through the wall, muffled German — Dietrich on the telephone. The radiator you're cuffed to ticks with heat. Somewhere outside, a church bell tolls the hour.

items.name: Hairpin
items.description: A thin metal hairpin. Bent just right, it could pick a simple lock.

then.text: Standard issue — Stasi secretaries wear these. Someone was in Dietrich's chair recently. The wire is thin enough to work inside a lock mechanism.
You bend it into an L-shape. Classic tension wrench configuration. Your training covered this.

items.name: Your Dossier
items.description: A manila folder stamped GEHEIM. Your cover identity — and how much the Stasi knows about you.

then.text: Subject: WEBER, ERNST (suspected alias). Cross-references to OPERATION LOOKING GLASS. They know your cover name but not your real one. Dietrich's handwritten note: 'Confirm handler identity — Checkpoint Charlie contact?' He's close. Too close.
Your file. Everything Dietrich knows. Everything he suspects. Destroying this would buy your network time — but not get you out.

You flick the lighter. The file catches fast — cheap East German paper. The flames consume Dietrich's notes, his cross-references, his suspicions. Smoke curls toward the ceiling. Your network is safe. Now save yourself.
You could tear it apart, but scraps can be reassembled. You need to destroy it completely.

items.name: Cipher Sheet
items.description: A one-time pad — rows of five-letter groups. Standard field encryption.

then.text: OTP-47B. Your own one-time pad — confiscated from you on capture. The groups are randomized but you recognize the format. Your handler uses the matching pad. With this and the right frequency, you can send an authenticated distress signal.
OTP-47B. Five-letter groups. Your handler, CARDINAL, holds the matching pad. Encode your message: station frequency, your agent number, extraction request.

items.name: Prisoner Transfer Forms
items.description: Blank Stasi transfer authorization forms. Bureaucracy might be your escape.

then.text: Form 17-B: Authorization for Prisoner Transfer Between Facilities. Requires: destination facility code, authorizing officer signature, and an official stamp. Three blanks to fill, three problems to solve.

items.name: Dietrich's Keys
items.description: A ring of brass keys. One for the door, one for the cabinet, others unknown.

then.text: Five keys on a plain ring. Two are standard door keys — one likely for this room. One small key fits a desk or cabinet lock. The other two are unmarked. Dietrich's entire domain on a ring.
American make — a Zippo, chrome finish. Engraved 'Berlin '58'. Dietrich's souvenir from the crisis? Or confiscated from another Western agent? It still works — the flame catches on the first strike.
Monogrammed K.D. — Klaus Dietrich. Contains three Juwel cigarettes and... something else. A thin strip taped inside the lid. Microfilm.
K.D.'s cigarette case. The microfilm is gone — you have it.
You carefully peel the microfilm strip from inside the lid. It's tiny — you'd need magnification to read it.

items.name: Microfilm Strip
items.description: A thin strip of photographic film. Too small to read with the naked eye.

then.text: Miniaturized photographs on a strip of film. The frames are impossibly small — you'd need a magnifying lens or a light source to read them. What was Dietrich hiding in his own cigarette case?

You hold the microfilm up and use the desk lamp lens to magnify it against the light. Names. Dates. Western agents Dietrich has been protecting — trading intelligence to both sides. The Oberst is a double agent. This is leverage. Pure, devastating leverage.

items.name: Magnifying Lens
items.description: A thick convex lens unscrewed from the desk lamp. Works as a crude magnifier.

then.text: A thick glass lens from the filing room desk lamp. Convex, decent magnification. Designed to focus light for reading, but it works as a loupe for anything small.

items.name: Official Ink Pad
items.description: A red ink pad bearing the Stasi district seal impression.

then.text: Red ink, well-saturated. The stamp impression reads: 'MINISTERIUM FÜR STAATSSICHERHEIT — BEZIRKSVERWALTUNG BERLIN'. The official seal of the Berlin district MfS office. With the right stamp, this makes any document look authentic.

items.name: Official Stamp
items.description: A wooden-handled rubber stamp. The seal of the Berlin Stasi district office.

then.text: Carved rubber on a wooden handle. Press it into the ink pad, then onto paper — instant bureaucratic authority. In East Germany, a stamp like this is more powerful than a gun.

items.name: Radio Codebook
items.description: Stasi radio operations codebook. Frequency assignments and call signs.

then.text: Field radio operations manual. Page after page of frequency assignments. You scan for anything useful... There — WESTERN MONITORING FREQUENCIES. The CIA listening post at Teufelsberg monitors 4.725 MHz continuously. Your handler CARDINAL would hear a coded message on that frequency within minutes.
4.725 MHz — the CIA listening post at Teufelsberg. CARDINAL monitors it.

items.name: Fountain Pen
items.description: Dietrich's Pelikan fountain pen. Blue-black ink, fine nib.

then.text: A Pelikan Souverän — expensive for an East German officer. Blue-black ink, fine nib. Dietrich's handwriting tool. Good enough to forge a signature if you've studied his hand.

items.name: Iron Pipe Section
items.description: A length of cast iron heating pipe. Heavy. About two feet long.

then.text: Cast iron, threaded at both ends. Two feet of solid metal. As a weapon it's devastating. As a pry bar it's crude but effective. The threading could even grip into masonry gaps.

items.name: Forged Transfer Papers
items.description: Transfer Form 17-B — filled out, signed, stamped. It looks authentic.

then.text: Prisoner WEBER, ERNST. Transfer to Hohenschönhausen facility for enhanced interrogation. Authorized by Oberst K. Dietrich. Stamped with the district seal. A guard who doesn't look too closely would process this without question.

combinations.message: You study Dietrich's handwriting from the notes in your file — the sharp angular K, the looping D. You fill in the transfer form: destination Hohenschönhausen, authorization Oberst Dietrich. The forgery isn't perfect, but in the right light, under the right pressure... it might pass.

You press the rubber stamp into the ink pad, then firmly onto the transfer form. The crimson seal of the Ministerium für Staatssicherheit blooms on the paper. Official. Unquestionable. The bureaucratic machinery of the state, turned against itself.

You hold the microfilm against the light and peer through the magnifying lens. Names swim into focus — Western agents Dietrich has been protecting. Dates of secret meetings. Dead drop locations. The Oberst is playing both sides. This changes everything.

objects.name: Cast Iron Radiator
objects.description: A heavy cast iron radiator bolted to the wall. Your right wrist is cuffed to it.

then.text: Soviet-made cast iron, bolted to the wall with four rusted brackets. The pipe connecting it runs up through the floor and into the ceiling. Your right wrist is handcuffed to the inlet pipe. The pipe itself is old — the threading where sections join is corroded.
The radiator ticks and hisses. The handcuffs dangle from the pipe where you left them. The connecting pipe section is old and corroded at the joints.

You pull against the cuffs. The metal bites into your wrist. The radiator doesn't budge — it's bolted solid. But the pipe... the pipe has some give where the sections thread together. You'd need a tool. Or a more delicate approach to the cuffs themselves.
You grip the pipe section and twist. The corroded threading grinds but gives slightly. With enough force — or a better grip — this section could come free.
You wrench the loosened pipe section free. Two feet of solid cast iron, threaded at both ends. Hot water dribbles from the broken joint. A weapon. A pry bar. Options.

You work the bent hairpin into the handcuff lock. Feel for the ratchet... there. Push against the pawl... click. The cuff springs open. Your wrist is raw and red but you're free. You pocket the hairpin — it might be useful again.
You can't reach the pipe section — you're cuffed to the radiator. Free yourself first.

objects.name: Handcuffs
objects.description: Standard Stasi-issue handcuffs. Your right wrist. The radiator pipe.

then.text: Standard handcuffs — single-lock ratchet mechanism. Mass-produced, nothing fancy. A pin or thin wire in the right hands could defeat this lock in seconds. Your training covered exactly this. You just need the right tool.
The cuffs dangle open from the radiator pipe. A souvenir of your captivity.
You twist and pull. The ratchet just tightens. Brute force won't work here — you need finesse. A thin piece of metal to work the lock mechanism.

objects.name: Metal Interrogation Table
objects.description: A heavy steel table bolted to the floor. Scratched, dented, stained.

then.text: Heavy steel, bolted to the concrete floor. The surface is scratched with years of desperate fingernails. A single ashtray sits in the center, still warm. Dietrich's notes are gone — he took them. But he left the ashtray and his pen.
You can barely reach the near edge. The cuffs hold you just short of the table's center.
Solid steel, bolted down. It's not going anywhere. The underside has scratches — previous occupants tried to loosen the bolts. They failed.

objects.name: Your Chair
objects.description: A wooden chair. You were sitting in it when you woke up.

then.text: Plain wooden chair, no padding. The back legs are slightly uneven — it rocks. Standard interrogation furniture: uncomfortable by design.

objects.name: Dietrich's Chair
objects.description: A padded leather chair. More comfortable than yours. A power statement.

then.text: Padded leather, brass rivets. Dietrich's chair — across the table from yours. The power dynamic is literal: comfort versus pain. Something glints on the floor beneath it — barely visible.

You circle behind the chair. A hairpin lies on the floor beneath it — must have fallen from whoever sat here before you. On the seat cushion, a slight impression. Dietrich sat here for hours. The leather still holds his warmth.
Dietrich's leather chair. You've already searched it.
You stretch toward Dietrich's chair. Your fingertips brush the floor beneath it... you feel something thin and metallic. A hairpin. You pull it toward you.
You search Dietrich's chair thoroughly. Under the seat cushion — nothing. But the hairpin on the floor... you pick it up.

objects.name: Overhead Light
objects.description: A single bare bulb on a long cord. It swings slightly.

then.text: A bare 60-watt bulb dangling from a cord. Classic interrogation lighting — the swinging motion is disorienting, casting shifting shadows. The cord runs to a switch by the door.
You reach up and stop the bulb from swinging. The shadows freeze. For a moment, the room feels almost normal. Then you let go and it resumes its pendulum.

objects.name: Wall Mirror
objects.description: A large mirror on the east wall. Standard interrogation room fixture.

then.text: Your reflection stares back — bruised, tired, but alive. The mirror is large, mounted flush against the wall. You press your fingernail to the glass. No gap between your nail and its reflection. Two-way mirror. Someone could be watching from the other side right now.
Two-way mirror. An observation room is on the other side. During Dietrich's phone call, nobody should be manning it — but you can't be sure.
You tap the mirror. It sounds hollow — the observation room is right behind it. But smashing it would make tremendous noise and the glass would shred you. There must be a better way.
You could shatter the mirror and break through to the observation room. But the noise would bring everyone running. The brute force approach — effective but desperate.

messages: You whisper toward the mirror: 'Is anyone watching?' No response. The observation room seems empty.
You speak softly to the glass: 'I know this is two-way.' Silence from the other side.
'If you can hear me...' Nothing. The room beyond is dark.

objects.name: Filing Cabinet
objects.description: A heavy steel filing cabinet against the north wall. Three drawers, one lock.

then.text: Standard-issue Stasi filing cabinet. Three drawers, master lock at the top. Labeled: AKTIV, ARCHIV, OPERATIV. This is where they keep the files — including, presumably, yours. There's a desk lamp on top, along with a typewriter and paper tray.
Locked. The master lock controls all three drawers. You'd need a key or a pick.
The smallest key on the ring slides into the cabinet lock. Click. All three drawers release.
You work the hairpin into the cabinet lock. Filing cabinet locks are simpler than handcuffs... there. The tumblers turn. All three drawers click free.

objects.name: Door
objects.description: A heavy steel door. Locked from the outside.

then.text: Steel-reinforced door, hinges on the outside. A deadbolt lock — keyed from both sides. Through the gap at the bottom, you can see the hallway. Fluorescent lights. The muffled sound of Dietrich's voice comes from the adjacent room.
Locked solid. The deadbolt is engaged. You'd need the key or something heavy enough to force it.
You try each key on the ring. The second one slides into the deadbolt. Turn. The bolt retracts with a heavy clunk. The door is unlocked. Freedom — or a hallway full of guards — is on the other side.

then.reason: You open the door and walk calmly into the hallway, transfer papers in hand. The guard at the end of the corridor stops you. 'Papers.' You hand over the forged Form 17-B. He squints at the seal, the signature, the facility code. 'Hohenschönhausen transfer. Late in the day for that.' You say nothing. He stamps your exit form and waves you through. You walk out the front door of a Stasi safe house carrying the most dangerous secret in East Berlin: the knowledge that Oberst Klaus Dietrich is a double agent. The cold October air has never tasted so sweet.

then.text: You crack the door open. A guard sits at the end of the corridor, reading a newspaper. He'd see you immediately. You need a disguise, papers, or a distraction.

then.reason: You ease the door open. The corridor is empty — the guard has gone to investigate. You move fast, silent, down the hall. Left turn. A fire exit. You push through into a rain-slicked alley. East Berlin stretches before you, gray and watchful. But you know these streets. In twenty minutes you'll be at the dead drop. In two hours, across the Wall. Dietrich will find an empty room and a mystery that will haunt him for years.

then.text: 'GUARD! I NEED WATER!' Silence. Then Dietrich's muffled voice: 'Patience. I'll be with you shortly.' Unhelpful, but now you know he's still on the phone.

You wedge the pipe section into the door frame and lever hard. The frame groans. One more hit — CRACK. The deadbolt tears through the frame. The door hangs open, splintered. The entire building heard that.

objects.name: Barred Window
objects.description: A small window with iron bars. Gray Berlin sky outside.

then.text: A narrow window. Iron bars set into the masonry. Through it you can see a courtyard, a wall, and beyond that — the rooftops of East Berlin. Second floor. The drop is survivable but the bars aren't moving without serious leverage.

objects.name: Propaganda Poster
objects.description: A large Socialist Unity Party poster on the south wall.

then.text: 'DER SOZIALISMUS SIEGT!' — Socialism Triumphs! A muscular worker shaking hands with a soldier. The poster is large — covering most of the south wall. The bottom right corner curls slightly. There's something behind it.

You peel the poster carefully from the wall. Behind it — a small wall safe, recessed into the plaster. Combination dial. Four numbers. Dietrich's personal safe, hidden behind the party's propaganda. How appropriate.
You can't reach the poster from here. You're cuffed to the radiator on the opposite wall.

objects.name: Hidden Wall Safe
objects.description: A small combination safe recessed into the wall behind the propaganda poster.

then.text: A Wertheim wall safe, pre-war manufacture. Four-number combination dial. Small enough for documents and personal effects. Dietrich went to some trouble to hide this — even from his own people. What's worth hiding from the Stasi inside a Stasi building?
The safe stands open. Empty now — you've taken everything.
The dial turns smoothly but you need four numbers. There must be a clue to the combination somewhere.

objects.name: Floor Vent
objects.description: A metal heating vent in the floor near the wall.

then.text: A rectangular heating vent set into the floor. Four flathead screws hold the grate in place. Through the slats you can see ductwork leading in two directions — one toward the radio room, another toward the street.
The screws are tight. Your fingers can't turn them. You need a flathead tool.
The pen nib is too wide and too fragile. It snaps immediately. Dietrich's Pelikan, ruined. But you still need a flathead tool.
You bend the hairpin flat and work it into the screw heads. Tedious, but one by one they turn. The grate lifts free. The duct is narrow — too small to crawl through, but you can reach inside.

You reach into the duct. Dust, dead insects... and voices. Distant, echoing through the metalwork. You can hear the radio room — someone tuning frequencies. And closer, from the adjacent room — Dietrich's voice, still on the phone. The duct carries sound both ways. Careful what you say.

objects.name: Coat Rack
objects.description: A wooden coat rack by the door. Dietrich's overcoat hangs from it.

then.text: A wooden coat rack, well-polished. Dietrich's gray wool overcoat hangs from the top hook. An officer's coat — heavy, well-tailored. Pockets.

You search Dietrich's overcoat. Left pocket: a monogrammed handkerchief. Right pocket: keys — a ring of brass keys. Inside breast pocket: a silver cigarette case and a Zippo lighter. Dietrich left his coat here when the phone rang. His mistake.
The coat rack is across the room. You can't reach it while cuffed to the radiator.
You've already emptied the pockets. Just the handkerchief remains.

objects.name: Dietrich's Briefcase
objects.description: A leather briefcase under the table. Brass combination latches.

then.text: Fine leather, brass hardware. Two combination latches — each with three digits. Dietrich's personal briefcase. He took his notes but left this under the table when the phone rang.
You stretch toward the briefcase under the table. You can just reach it with your foot, but you can't manipulate the latches from here.
The combination latches are set to 000-000. You try various combinations but nothing clicks. There must be a clue to the code somewhere.
The briefcase is open. You've already taken everything useful.

objects.name: Ashtray
objects.description: A heavy glass ashtray. Two cigarette butts, still warm.

then.text: Heavy crystal glass. Two Juwel cigarette butts — Dietrich's brand. One is still faintly warm. On the bottom of the ashtray, scratched into the glass with a sharp edge: '1-9-6-1'. A date? A code? Dietrich absently scratched it during interrogation. Nineteen sixty-one — the year the Wall went up.
The numbers scratched on the bottom: 1-9-6-1. The year the Berlin Wall went up. Significant to Dietrich somehow.
Too heavy and conspicuous to carry. But the number scratched in the bottom — that's useful.

objects.name: Telephone
objects.description: A black Bakelite telephone on a wall bracket near the door.

then.text: Standard Post Office model. The dial has numbers 0-9 and a district exchange label. It's an internal line — you could call other extensions in the building, but not outside. The cord stretches to the wall bracket.
You pick up the receiver. A dial tone. You could dial an internal extension — maybe create a distraction? The guard post would be extension 1. Dietrich's office is extension 3.
The telephone is by the door — far out of reach while you're cuffed.

You dial extension 1 — the guard post. It rings twice. 'Wache.' Guard speaking. You deepen your voice: 'Checkpoint breach alert. All guards to the front entrance immediately.' A pause. 'Jawohl!' The phone clicks dead. Footsteps in the corridor, receding fast. The corridor guard is gone.

effects.text: Footsteps return to the corridor. The false alarm has been discovered. The guard is back at his post — and suspicious.

objects.name: Top Drawer (AKTIV)
objects.description: The top drawer of the filing cabinet. Labeled 'AKTIV' — active cases.

then.text: You slide open the top drawer. Active case files — dozens of manila folders. You flip through: WEBER, ERNST. That's your cover name. Your dossier.
The drawer is locked. The master lock controls all three drawers.
Active case files. You've already taken your dossier. The other files are other people's nightmares — you leave them.

objects.name: Middle Drawer (ARCHIV)
objects.description: The middle drawer. Labeled 'ARCHIV' — archived cases.

then.text: The archive drawer. Closed cases — some marked 'ERLEDIGT' (resolved), others 'VERSTORBEN' (deceased). Behind the files, pushed to the back: blank prisoner transfer forms. Form 17-B, a stack of them. And next to them — a rubber stamp and an ink pad.
Locked.

objects.name: Bottom Drawer (OPERATIV)
objects.description: The bottom drawer. Labeled 'OPERATIV' — operational materials.

then.text: Operational materials. Cipher sheets, codebooks, field manuals. And there — your own cipher sheet, confiscated at capture. OTP-47B. Your one-time pad. If you can reach a radio and the right frequency, this is your lifeline to the West.
Locked.

objects.name: Paper Tray
objects.description: A metal paper tray on top of the cabinet.

then.text: Blank paper and carbon sheets. Stasi bureaucracy runs on paper — everything in triplicate. Nothing remarkable here.

objects.name: Desk Lamp
objects.description: An adjustable desk lamp on top of the filing cabinet.

then.text: A green-shaded adjustable desk lamp. The lens is a thick convex glass — magnifying type, for reading fine print. It unscrews from the shade assembly.
You unscrew the magnifying lens from the lamp shade. Thick glass, good optics. Useful for reading anything small — like microfilm.
The desk lamp, minus its lens. Still works as a light, but the magnifying capability is in your pocket now.

objects.name: Typewriter
objects.description: An Optima typewriter. Standard Stasi office equipment.

then.text: An Optima Elite — East German manufacture. A fresh sheet of paper is loaded. The ribbon is inked. Ready to type. Every Stasi typewriter has a unique type signature — like fingerprints for machines. Anything typed here could be traced to this office.

You consider typing the transfer form on the typewriter — more official than handwriting. But every Stasi typewriter is registered. This one's type signature would trace directly to this office. Handwriting is safer — Dietrich's handwriting, specifically. Forge it by hand.
You tap a key. The letter strikes the paper with a sharp clack. Loud. Official. But you have nothing to type right now.

objects.name: Radio Transceiver
objects.description: A military-grade shortwave radio. The Stasi's ears and mouth.

then.text: A Funkwerk Köpenick SE-300 shortwave transceiver. Military grade. Frequency range covers HF bands — including the ones Western intelligence monitors. The power switch is on the left, frequency dial on the right. A Morse key sits below the main unit.
You flip the power switch. The radio hums to life. Tubes glow warm orange behind the faceplate. The frequency dial reads 3.500 MHz — a Stasi operational channel. You need to tune it.
You flip the switch. Nothing. The power is out — Western sabotage knocked the building's electricity. The radio is dead until power returns.

You encode your message using the one-time pad. Agent LOOKING GLASS. Position compromised. Request immediate extraction. Checkpoint Charlie, dawn. You tap it out on the Morse key, one careful dit-dah at a time. The signal goes out into the ether — toward Teufelsberg, toward CARDINAL, toward home.

You have the cipher sheet but you don't know what frequency CARDINAL monitors. Sending on a random frequency would be pointless — or intercepted by the wrong people. You need to find the frequency first.

objects.name: Frequency Dial
objects.description: The radio's main tuning dial. Currently set to a Stasi channel.

then.text: A large tuning dial graduated in MHz. Currently set to 3.500 — a Stasi operational channel. The dial covers 2.000 to 8.000 MHz.

You turn the dial slowly to 4.725 MHz. The CIA listening post at Teufelsberg. Static gives way to silence — the frequency is monitored continuously but quiet. They're listening. Now you need your cipher sheet to send an authenticated message.
You turn the dial through the frequencies. Static, voices in German, coded transmissions, more static. Without knowing the exact frequency your handler monitors, you're scanning blind.

objects.name: Morse Key
objects.description: A brass telegraph key for sending Morse code.

then.text: A standard straight key — brass contacts on a Bakelite base. Your Morse is rusty but adequate. Dit-dah, dit-dah. The muscle memory is still there.
You tap the key. No sound — the radio isn't powered on.
The message has been sent. Sending again risks interception. CARDINAL heard you. Now you need to survive until dawn.

objects.name: Codebook Shelf
objects.description: A narrow shelf of radio operations manuals and codebooks.

then.text: Technical manuals for the SE-300 transceiver. Frequency allocation tables. And — a Stasi radio codebook. Field edition, current month. Frequency assignments for every monitoring station in the Eastern Bloc... and, more importantly, the frequencies they've identified as Western.
You slip the codebook off the shelf. This is intelligence gold — but right now you need it for one specific thing: finding the frequency your handler monitors.

objects.name: Antenna Cable
objects.description: A coaxial cable running from the radio to the roof antenna.

then.text: Coaxial cable, running from the transceiver up through the ceiling to a rooftop antenna. The connection is solid. Without this, the radio can receive but not transmit — its signal wouldn't reach past the building.

objects.name: Radio Logbook
objects.description: A hardbound logbook of radio transmissions, dates and times.

then.text: A log of all radio transmissions from this station. Dates, times, frequencies, operators. You scan the recent entries... One stands out. Three nights ago, 02:00: an unauthorized transmission on 4.725 MHz. Duration: 47 seconds. Operator: 'KD'. Klaus Dietrich. Transmitting to a Western frequency in the middle of the night. The Oberst has a secret of his own.
The logbook. Dietrich's unauthorized transmission: 4.725 MHz. He's been talking to the West.

objects.name: Window Bars
objects.description: Iron bars set into the window frame masonry.

then.text: Four iron bars, 20mm diameter, set into the window frame masonry. The mortar around the bottom of two bars looks slightly cracked — old building, decades of freeze-thaw cycles. With enough leverage applied to the weakest point...
You grip the bars and pull. They don't move. The iron is solid — it's the mortar that's weak. You'd need a lever.

You wedge the pipe section between two bars and lever hard. The mortar around the weakest bar cracks, crumbles. You work the pipe back and forth — more mortar falls. The bar loosens. One more pull — it tears free from the frame. Then the next one. A gap wide enough to squeeze through.
Two bars are gone. The gap is tight but passable. A two-story drop to the courtyard below. The wall on the far side is topped with wire — but there's a drain pipe that might hold your weight.

objects.name: Window Glass
objects.description: Double-pane glass behind the bars.

then.text: Double-pane glass, sealed shut. Through it: a gray courtyard, a boundary wall, East Berlin rooftops. Freedom, thirty feet away and two stories down.
With the bars gone, you can reach the glass. You wrap your fist in your sleeve and punch. The glass shatters outward. Cold Berlin air rushes in, carrying the smell of rain and diesel.

then.reason: You squeeze through the gap where the bars were, drop to the courtyard, and run. The drain pipe holds your weight over the wall. You hit the alley on the other side running. East Berlin at night — dangerous, but you know these streets. You have a dead drop location, a compromised identity to shed, and a border to cross. But you're alive, you're free, and you carry Oberst Dietrich's secret with you. By morning, you'll be in the West.

objects.name: Window Ledge
objects.description: The narrow stone ledge inside the window frame.

then.text: A narrow stone ledge. Pigeon droppings and old mortar dust. Something is scratched into the stone — tiny letters. Previous occupant's message? You'd need to look closer.

You brush away the dust and trace the scratches with your finger. Numbers: '19-08-61'. August 19, 1961 — six days after the Wall went up. And below: 'ES GIBT IMMER EINEN WEG' — There is always a way. Someone left you a message across the decades.

objects.name: Wall Crack
objects.description: A long crack running through the plaster near the window.

then.text: A crack in the plaster, running from floor to ceiling. The building is pre-war — bombing damage never properly repaired. The plaster hides old brickwork. Some of these bricks might be loose, especially where the crack is widest near the heating pipe.
You pick at the plaster around the crack. Chunks fall away, revealing old red brick beneath. The mortar between bricks is crumbling. This wall has been wanting to fall for twenty years.

You swing the pipe into the exposed brickwork. Once. Twice. Bricks shift and tumble. The old mortar disintegrates. A section of wall gives way — daylight streams through. A hole just large enough to crawl through, opening onto the building's exterior wall. Two stories up, but a drain pipe runs right past the opening.

then.reason: You squeeze through the breach in the wall. The cold air hits you immediately. You grab the drain pipe and lower yourself, hand over hand, to the alley below. Rain-slicked cobblestones. You're outside. You're free. The hole in the wall will tell Dietrich everything he needs to know — that his prisoner escaped, and more importantly, that his building's walls are as rotten as the state they serve.

objects.name: Heating Pipe
objects.description: A vertical heating pipe running along the window wall.

then.text: A vertical cast iron pipe, part of the building's heating system. It connects to the radiator in the main room through the wall. The threaded joints are corroded, just like the radiator connection.
You twist the pipe at the joint. It moves — barely. The threads are corroded but not fused. With sustained effort, this section could come free.

objects.name: Plaster Wall Section
objects.description: A large section of plaster wall between the crack and the window.

then.text: Water-stained plaster. The surface is bubbled and peeling — decades of neglect. The wall behind it is old brick, potentially compromised by the crack running through it.
You push against the plaster. It flexes slightly — the underlying brick isn't solid. But you'd need to expose the brick first through the crack to do any real damage.

objects.name: Cabinet Lock
objects.description: A sturdy lock mechanism on the filing cabinet.

states.locked: The lock is engaged, securing the cabinet drawers.
states.unlocked: The lock has been picked open.

then.text: A standard East German filing cabinet lock. Nothing fancy, but solid enough.
The lock won't budge without a tool.
You work the hairpin into the lock mechanism. After some careful manipulation, it clicks open.

on_solve.text: 1-9-6-1. The year the Wall went up. The tumblers align. Click. The safe door swings open. Inside: a Walther PPK pistol, a codebook, and a sealed envelope addressed to a West Berlin post office box. Dietrich's insurance policy.

8-1-3. Click-click. Both latches release. Inside: a Pelikan fountain pen, interrogation notes in Dietrich's angular handwriting, and — your personal effects bag. They took everything when you were captured.

config.wrong_step_message: Wrong sequence. The radio protocol resets.

on_solve.text: Power — tune — encode — transmit. The sequence completes. Your coded message pulses across the airwaves. Somewhere at Teufelsberg, an analyst sits up straight. Agent LOOKING GLASS is alive. Extraction protocol activates.

on_solve.reason: The message is sent. You destroy the cipher sheet and wait. Forty-seven minutes later, an explosion rocks the building — a diversionary charge on the east wall. In the chaos, a man in a Stasi uniform appears at your door. 'CARDINAL sends regards,' he whispers in English. He hands you a coat, an ID card, and a pistol. You walk out through the smoke and confusion. By dawn, you're at Checkpoint Charlie. By noon, you're in the West, debriefing over coffee and American cigarettes. Oberst Dietrich will spend the next month explaining how a prisoner vanished from a locked room during a building-wide emergency that nobody authorized.

on_fail.text: The sequence is wrong. You'll need to start over.

phases.name: Interrogation

on_enter.text: Your head throbs. Your right wrist aches where the handcuff bites. Through the wall, Dietrich's voice — rapid German on the telephone. He stepped out to take a call. How long ago? Minutes? You're alone. For now.

phases.ambient_text: Muffled conversation through the wall. The radiator ticks. A church bell, distant.

phases.name: Unattended

on_enter.text: Free from the cuffs. Your wrist is raw but functional. The room opens up — filing cabinet, coat rack, telephone, door. Dietrich's world, yours to search. Work fast. He won't be on the phone forever.

phases.ambient_text: The telephone conversation next door grows quieter. Dietrich is wrapping up.

phases.name: Escape Attempt

on_enter.text: Dietrich's phone call has ended. Footsteps in the corridor. He's coming back — and he'll see immediately that something is wrong. Whatever your plan is, execute it now.

phases.ambient_text: Footsteps. Approaching. Time is a knife edge.

effects.text: Footsteps in the corridor — a guard change. You hear two voices, then one set of steps walking away. A brief window where the new guard settles in, checks his paperwork.
Through the wall, Dietrich's voice rises — then silence. The phone call is over. You hear a chair scrape back. He's standing up.
Dietrich's footsteps approach the door. The knob turns. He's coming in.

The lights die. Total darkness for three seconds — then emergency lighting kicks in, bathing everything in red. Muffled shouting from below. The power has been cut. Western sabotage? Or just East German infrastructure? Either way, the building is running on backup power. Some systems won't work.
The main lights flicker back on. Power restored. The confusion downstairs continues — you hear Dietrich barking orders.

"The handcuffs are empty." Dietrich's voice is ice. "Impressive. I underestimated you." His calm is more terrifying than rage. "But this building has no exits I don't control. Shall we discuss your options?"
"My filing cabinet. Open." Dietrich's voice drops to a whisper. "You've been reading. How much do you know?" For the first time, you hear something new in his voice. Fear.

killer.name: Oberst Klaus Dietrich
killer.description: Stasi intelligence officer. Methodical, intellectual, coldly polite. Quotes Schiller and Kant between interrogation questions. Plays chess against himself. Respects worthy opponents — which makes him more dangerous, not less.

on_approach: I trust you've been comfortable in my absence.
Schiller wrote: 'Against stupidity, the gods themselves contend in vain.' Let's see if you're an exception.
Time for another round, I think.
on_search: I know you're here. The building is sealed.
This is unnecessary. You cannot leave. We both know this.
Every fugitive makes the same mistake — they confuse movement with progress.
I'll find you. I always do. It's simply a matter of patience.
on_clear: Behaving yourself. Good. We'll resume shortly.
Mm. Everything in order. For now.
I'll be back. Don't go anywhere.
on_evidence: Resourceful. I expected no less from a Western operative.
So. The game changes. Very well.
You should not have touched my things.
on_catch: The game is over. Shall I tell you where you went wrong?
You played well. Not well enough.

effects.text: You hear the filing cabinet lock click. Dietrich has relocked it on his way out.
"My poster," Dietrich mutters. "And my safe exposed. You are thorough." His search becomes more intense.

special_behaviors.description: Dietrich is occupied with a phone call in the adjacent room.
Power outage creates building-wide chaos. Dietrich is managing the situation.

win_conditions.description: Send coded message to Western handler via radio for extraction
Walk out the front door with forged transfer papers
Break through window bars and escape
Breach the weakened wall and escape
Distract the guard and escape through the unlocked door

lose_conditions.description: Dietrich finds you during a search
Run out of time — Dietrich's superiors arrive for the formal interrogation
lose_conditions.message: A car pulls up outside. Doors slam. Heavy footsteps on the stairs. Dietrich's voice: 'Ah, Generalmajor. The prisoner is ready.' Three men in dark suits enter the room. The formal interrogation begins. There will be no escape from this one.

hints.text: You're handcuffed to the radiator. Look around — even from here, you might be able to reach something useful near Dietrich's chair.
Something glints on the floor under Dietrich's chair. Try reaching for it with your free hand.
The hairpin could pick the handcuff lock. Use it on the handcuffs or the radiator.
Dietrich left in a hurry — his overcoat is still on the rack. Check the pockets.
Dietrich's keys should open the filing cabinet. Your file — and other useful things — are inside.
That propaganda poster on the south wall — the corner is peeling. What's behind it?
The wall safe needs a 4-digit combination. Dietrich scratched something into the ashtray on the table — have you looked at it?
You have your cipher sheet. Look at the filing cabinet closeup — there's a radio room accessible. Find the right frequency and transmit.
Transfer forms, a stamp, an ink pad, and Dietrich's pen. Study his handwriting from your file and forge the papers.
The window bars, the cracked wall — either could be your way out if you have a strong enough lever. The heating pipe section from the radiator might work.

solution_paths.name: The Signal
solution_paths.description: Send a coded distress message to your CIA handler via radio. Spy tradecraft path — quiet, precise, professional.
steps: Find hairpin under Dietrich's chair (hand on chair_dietrich while handcuffed)
Pick handcuff lock (use hairpin on radiator)
Search Dietrich's coat for keys (hand on coat_rack)
Unlock filing cabinet (use dietrich_keys on filing_cabinet)
Open bottom drawer (OPERATIV) to get cipher_sheet
Navigate to radio room (look at filing cabinet to enter closeup, then access radio_closeup)
Find radio frequency: either examine radio logbook (4.725 MHz) OR get codebook from safe/shelf
Power on radio (hand on radio_transceiver)
Tune to 4.725 MHz (hand on frequency_dial with knows_radio_frequency flag)
Use cipher_sheet on radio to encode and transmit message
OR complete the cipher_decode sequence puzzle

solution_paths.name: The Forgery
solution_paths.description: Forge prisoner transfer papers and walk out the front door. Turn the Stasi's own bureaucracy against them.
steps: Find hairpin, pick handcuffs (as above)
Search Dietrich's coat for keys
Unlock filing cabinet
Open top drawer — get your dossier (study Dietrich's handwriting)
Open middle drawer — get transfer forms, rubber stamp, ink pad
Open briefcase (combination 8-1-3, clue from window ledge inscription 19-08-61) to get pen
Combine transfer_forms + pen (requires stamp_found, ink_pad_found, found_your_file flags)
Combine forged_papers + ink_pad (requires rubber_stamp) to stamp them
Unlock door with Dietrich's keys
Walk through door with stamped forged papers

solution_paths.name: The Breach
solution_paths.description: Break out through the window or wall using brute force. Loud, fast, desperate.
steps: Find hairpin, pick handcuffs
Loosen heating pipe (hand on radiator after freeing, then hand on heating_pipe in window_closeup)
Remove pipe section from radiator
Navigate to window closeup
EITHER: Break window bars with pipe_section, then break glass, then climb out
OR: Expose brick through wall crack (hand on wall_crack), then breach wall with pipe_section, then climb through
Optional: Use telephone to distract guard first (talk on telephone), then escape through door
